title: The poets
hook: the surah's name, and the poets excepted who believe, do good and remember Allah (26:224–227)

segments.voice: Yesterday: khafd al-janah, lowering the wing in gentleness. Your line was lower the wing.

In the Arabia the Prophet grew up in, the old histories describe the poet as no quiet figure with a notebook. A poet could be a weapon and a newspaper at once. A tribe's poet praised his own people and mocked their rivals, and a sharp line could travel from camp to camp and stick to a family's name. So when the Prophet began reciting the Qur'an, some opponents had a label ready: he's just a poet. Surah Ash-Shu'ara, named for the poets, ends by answering that.

The surah's last verses don't flatter the poets of that time. Those who go astray follow them. They wander in every valley, chasing any mood or theme, and they say what they don't do. Commentators read this as the answer to the label: the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, they say, was not wandering, and did what he said. Elsewhere the Qur'an says plainly that it is not the word of a poet. Then, in the very last verse, a turn: except those who believe, and do good works, and remember God much, and defend themselves after they have been wronged. So the surah doesn't ban poetry. It sorts it: words that wander, and words that remember. The exception had faces. The Prophet had poets among his companions, Hassan ibn Thabit among them. A report in Bukhari says the Prophet asked Hassan to answer the Quraysh's satires in verse, and prayed that God support him with the Holy Spirit, which Muslims understand as the angel Jibril. Another hadith in Bukhari says some poetry is wisdom. Later, Ka'b ibn Zuhayr, a poet who had written against the Prophet, came and recited a famous ode, and tradition says the Prophet gave him his own cloak; scholars discuss the strength of that story's chains. From those beginnings grew a long tradition of praise poems for the Prophet, in Arabic and many other languages, sung at weddings and gatherings. The surah's test is simple: do the words remember God, and do the people saying them live them?

segments.voice: If you know a devotional poem by heart, a line of a nasheed, a verse someone once sang to you, a praise poem from your own language, let it play slowly in your mind and notice what it does to your breathing. If none comes, sit with the surah's own words instead: those who believe, and remember God much. Notice which line you'd want to keep, and if you pray, say it as a prayer.
The poets. Ash-Shu'ara, the surah named for them, which turns away the poets who wander and keeps the ones who believe, do good and remember God much. Today's word.
Your line: words that remember. Poetry can wander, or it can remember. That's day five hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: Muslims across the world sing and recite devotional poetry, from Arabic odes praising the Prophet to nasheeds and qawwali, while scholars hold that the Qur'an itself is not poetry.

chat.says: Does the Qur'an say poetry is bad?
options: No. It sorts it: words that wander, and words that believe and remember God.
Yes. Ash-Shu'ara forbids poetry, and the Prophet never allowed any of it.
No. It praises the Prophet as the greatest poet of the Arabs.
chat.meaning: The surah's last verse makes an exception for poets who believe, do good and remember God, and Hassan ibn Thabit answered in verse at the Prophet's request.

Hassan ibn Thabit.meaning: a companion of the Prophet who answered in verse

Ka'b ibn Zuhayr.meaning: a poet who once wrote against the Prophet, then came to him

notes: All Qur'an and hadith paraphrased. Bukhari numbers (3212 for Hassan, 6145 for 'some poetry is wisdom') cited from memory; confirm.
The Holy Spirit (ruh al-qudus) understood as Jibril: standard Sunni reading; confirm.
Ka'b ibn Zuhayr's cloak (burda): presented as tradition with debated chains; confirm.
Original note: sha'ir from sh-'-r, to perceive/know (cf. lexicons); confirm.
